newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia's Hun Sen says may drop bid to join ASEAN.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's Hun Sen says may drop bid to join ASEAN.

text.p: Cambodia's Second Prime Minister Hun Sen said on Monday he might drop Cambodia's bid to join the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) and warned big powers not to use aid as a weapon to pressure him.
Hun Sen's rejection of intervention in Cambodia's internal affairs came as King Norodom Sihanouk said he doubted that efforts by foreign envoys to negotiate an end to Cambodia's crisis would succeed.
"We consider if we go to ASEAN or if we stop. I want to stop if ASEAN continues to interfere in our internal affairs," Hun Sen told reporters in Kompong Thom province, north of the capital.
The seven-member group last week postponed Cambodia's membership indefinitely in response to Hun Sen's ouster of First Prime Minster Prince Norodom Ranariddh on July 6.
"I am afraid of joining ASEAN because of ASEAN interference in internal affairs," he said.
ASEAN groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam. Cambodia had been due to join this month with Laos and Burma.
ASEAN said last week it still recognised Ranariddh as first prime minister and would try to work out a ceasefire between forces loyal to the rival premiers.
Hun Sen warned Cambodia's aid donors not to try to pressure him with threats of aid cuts.
"You cannot come and say 'Excellency, you must do this or do that because my country has helped you a lot'," Hun Sen said of aid donors.
Cambodia gets half its annual budget from overseas donations.

King Sihanouk said on Monday he was doubtful that efforts by ASEAN, as well as by France, the United States and Japan, to push for a negotiated settlement to Cambodia's crisis, would succeed in the light of Hun Sen's rejection of an earlier offer to hold reconciliation talks.
The king, who is in Beijing for medical treatment, said he was willing to meet envoys from ASEAN and the three countries who he said were due in Beijing this week.

Sihanouk and the envoys were "not authorised by 'The Strongman' (Hun Sen) to intervene in that which is called the internal affairs of Cambodia", the king said in an interview with his information bulletin, released by the palace on Monday.
Sihanouk called on his son Ranariddh and Hun Sen to meet him in Beijing for mediation talks after their forces began fighting in the capital on July 5.
The next day, as Hun Sen's troops were pushing Ranariddh's men out of the Phnom Penh, Hun Sen announced Ranariddh's ouster and said bluntly there was no need for the king's mediation talks.
Hun Sen has told members of Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party remaining in Cambodia to choose a new first prime minister. He has said he does not want to become first prime minister.
Hun Sen said Ranariddh should be prosecuted for illegal negotiations with the Khmer Rouge guerrilla group and his alleged illegal import of weapons.

On Monday he said he was taking steps to have the prince, who is overseas seeking to gather foreign support, brought back for trial and asking Cambodian legal authorities to prepare an international warrant for his arrest.
"I would like to suggest to the Cambodian court to prepare the documents in order to sentence Ranariddh and then send the arresting summons abroad," he said.
Sihanouk indicated on Sunday that he would not endorse Cambodia's new government, but stopped short of accusing Hun Sen of staging a coup.
Foreign Minister Ung Huot, a member of Ranariddh's royalist FUNCINPEC party, returned to Cambodia on Monday saying he wanted to work for democracy and pluralism.
Many FUNCINPEC members and sympathisers fled from the country in the aftermath of Ranariddh's ouster and the execution of Ho Sok, a FUNCINPEC secretary of state at the interior ministry.
Hun Sen confirmed on Monday that Chao Sambath, a FUNCINPEC intelligence officer, had also been killed in the recent fighting.
Opposition leader Sam Rainsy, an ally of Ranariddh, was due to return to Cambodia overland from Thailand on Monday, opposition and Thai army sources said.
King Sihanouk on Monday also condemned any alliance with Khmer Rouge guerrilla factions.
The Khmer Rouge, responsible for the death of more than a million Cambodians during their 1975-79 rule, has recently split into several factions.

"These Khmer Rouge have committed unforgivable crimes against humanity. It is very immoral to use them in this very ugly struggle for power which has cost so much loss, ruin, misery suffering and despair to our innocent little people," he said.
Ranariddh announced in May that he had opened negotiations with the Khmer Rouge in an effort to end their war against the government.

The prince also said he would be willing to form a political alliance with the group's main political leader, Khieu Samphan, if he announced he had broken with supreme leader Pol Pot and recognised the Cambodian constitution.

Hun Sen justified his forces' move against Ranariddh's men in the capital by saying Ranariddh's military commanders were smuggling defectors from the Khmer Rouge into the city to bolster the prince's troop strength. Ranariddh denied he was doing so. Meanwhile, sources said Cambodia's rag-tag opposition army is staging a desperate retreat into the country's jungles.

Soldiers loyal to Ranariddh are withdrawing into northwestern Cambodia along with some Khmer Rouge forces, laying mines, blowing up bridges and counting on the rainy season to delay pursuing government troops.
Outnumbered, harried by sporadic government rocket and artillery fire, the opposition army seems keen to retreat and regroup rather than stand and fight.
